title: What fills the space

cards: An hour without the phone has a way of turning up a visitor. Not peace, at first. Something itchier.
Around minute ten, for some people, a restless flatness: nothing to do, nothing to look at, the clock suddenly very slow. A shelf gets reorganized. Someone stands in front of the fridge with no plan.
The visitor's name is boredom, and a phone in the pocket makes it easy never to meet it for long. Today, a long look at it.

teach.b: In the sixteen hundreds, the French mathematician Blaise Pascal wrote a line that sounds like it was written about phones.

He said he'd discovered that all of people's unhappiness comes from one thing, "that they cannot stay quietly in their own chamber." We chase distractions, he said, so we never have to sit alone with ourselves.
In 2014, psychologists tested this almost literally.

teach.h: THE BUTTON IN THE EMPTY ROOM.
teach.b: They asked people to sit alone in a plain room for six to fifteen minutes with nothing but their thoughts. Many found it unpleasant.

In one version, people could press a button to give themselves a mild electric shock, and a surprising number did, rather than just sit there: about two in three men, and one in four women. Boredom is uncomfortable.
That's real. But there's another side.

In a different study, people who first did something dull, copying numbers out of a phone book, then came up with more creative ideas than people who hadn't. Boredom seems to push the mind to go looking.
So boredom isn't the end of the story. It's the hallway.
Here's the bet this week's practice makes: if you don't grab the phone, the restlessness peaks, and then, slowly, the mind starts to notice things. The sound of the fridge. The light on the wall.
A thought you haven't had time for in months. What fills the space isn't nothing. Often it's you.
Bored is the door. The only trick is waiting long enough to walk through.

how: People who try a screen-free stretch often describe restless boredom at first, followed by more noticing and daydreaming, and some deliberately let themselves be bored instead of reaching for a device.

o: to be empty, to be free
to be tired, to need sleep
to be bored, to be restless

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.
p: can't stay quietly in a room

s: in the 2014 study, nobody chose a shock over sitting alone
about two in three men and one in four women pressed the button.
doing something dull first led to more creative ideas in one study
people who copied numbers from a phone book came up with more ideas.
boredom just gets worse the longer you sit with it
the restlessness peaks, then the mind starts to notice things.

games.q: you're alone in a plain room for fifteen minutes. there's a button that gives a mild shock. what did many people in the study do?
games.why: a surprising number pressed it, rather than just sit with their thoughts. Pascal would not have been surprised.

practice: Just sit, eyes open, and let it be dull: don't follow your breath, don't count, don't do anything clever. Notice the itch to do something, let it rise, and don't scratch it.
Then watch what comes after, a sound, a color, a thought, whatever fills the space.

wordCard.voice: Vacare, the Latin root of vacant and vacation, meaning to be empty, to be free. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: to be empty, to be free. the root of vacation, and of vacant: time with nothing in it.

carryVoice: Your line: bored is the door. On the other side, the noticing starts. Day one hundred forty-five, done.
